name: Mental Maths: 2-Digit Subtraction
description: A focused KaTeX-enabled mental-arithmetic deck for subtracting two-digit numbers. It develops direct place-value subtraction, borrowing, bridge-to-ten, compensation, counting up, complements to 100, estimation, error detection, and strategy selection.
estimatedTime: 100–130 minutes for the first pass; then 10–15 minute review bursts

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: What is the default mental route?
cards.definition:
Subtract tens first, then ones.

$$
\begin{aligned}
76 - 42 \\
&= 76 - 40 - 2 \\
&= 36 - 2 \\
&= 34
\end{aligned}
$$
Use this when the ones digit is large enough and no faster pattern is obvious.

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: When is direct subtraction easiest?
cards.definition:
Use direct subtraction when no borrowing is needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
86 - 43 \\
&= 86 - 40 - 3 \\
&= 46 - 3 \\
&= 43
\end{aligned}
$$
Here, 6 ≥ 3, so the ones can be removed directly.

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: What does borrowing mean mentally?
cards.definition:
When the ones digit is too small, trade one ten for ten ones.

$$
\begin{aligned}
52 - 38 \\
&= 40 + 12 - 30 - 8 \\
&= 10 + 4 \\
&= 14
\end{aligned}
$$
The key idea is not a mysterious rule: 52 = 40 + 12.

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: When should you count up instead?
cards.definition:
Count up when the two numbers are close or when the smaller number is close to a clean ten or hundred.

$$
\begin{aligned}
63 - 58 \\
58 \to 60 &= 2 \\
60 \to 63 &= 3 \\
63 - 58 &= 2+3=5
\end{aligned}
$$
This can be easier than borrowing.

Round the number being subtracted to a friendly ten, then correct the difference.

$$
\begin{aligned}
84 - 29 \\
&= 84 - 30 + 1 \\
&= 54 + 1 \\
&= 55
\end{aligned}
$$
Subtracting 30 removes 1 too much, so add 1 back.

Use it when the starting number is just above a ten.

$$
\begin{aligned}
43 - 18 \\
&= 43 - 3 - 15 \\
&= 40 - 15 \\
&= 25
\end{aligned}
$$
First reach a friendly ten, then finish.

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: When is subtraction from 100 easiest?
cards.definition:
Use complements when subtracting from 100.

$$
\begin{aligned}
100 - 37 &= 63 \\
37 + 63 &= 100
\end{aligned}
$$
Think: What pairs with 37 to make 100?

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: How do you subtract from a multiple of 10?
cards.definition:
Treat the multiple of 10 as tens and ones.

$$
\begin{aligned}
70 - 46 \\
&= 60 + 10 - 40 - 6 \\
&= 20 + 4 \\
&= 24
\end{aligned}
$$
This is borrowing from the tens place.

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: How do you use a near-double?
cards.definition:
When two numbers are close, use the gap rather than full subtraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}
49 - 47 &= 2 \\
73 - 71 &= 2
\end{aligned}
$$
For close numbers, the distance is often visible faster than a formal method.

Estimation catches implausible answers.

Example:
87 − 39 is about 90 − 40 = 50.

So an exact answer near 48 is plausible. An answer such as 58 deserves a recheck.

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: Which method is best for 84 − 29?
cards.definition:
Compensation.

$$
\begin{aligned}
84-29 \\
&=84-30+1 \\
&=55
\end{aligned}
$$
The correction is only 1.

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: Which method is best for 63 − 58?
cards.definition:
Counting up.

$$
\begin{aligned}
58\to60 &=2 \\
60\to63 &=3 \\
63-58 &=5
\end{aligned}
$$
The gap is small and the bridge through 60 is easy.

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: Which method is best for 76 − 42?
cards.definition:
Direct tens-and-ones subtraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}
76-42 \\
&=76-40-2 \\
&=34
\end{aligned}
$$
No borrowing or compensation is needed.

cards.term: 2-Digit Subtraction: When should you not force a shortcut?
cards.definition:
Use direct subtraction when a shortcut creates extra correction work.

Example:
76 − 42 is already simple as 76 − 40 − 2.

Efficient mental maths means choosing the least demanding accurate route.

cards.definition:
50 is better.

87 ≈ 90 and 39 ≈ 40, so
90 − 40 = 50.

The exact answer is 48.

40 is better.

64 ≈ 60 and 29 ≈ 30, so
60 − 30 = 30.

The exact answer is 35, making 40 closer than 20.

cards.term: True or false: Counting up is always faster than borrowing.
cards.definition:
False.

Counting up is excellent for small gaps, such as 63 − 58. But for 86 − 43, direct subtraction is faster:
86 − 40 − 3 = 43.

cards.term: True or false: A compensation correction must always be added back.
cards.definition:
False.

If you round the subtrahend up, add the difference back:
84 − 29 = 84 − 30 + 1.

If you round it down, subtract the difference:
62 − 31 = 62 − 30 − 1.
